cards.title: Volumetric Video's Walls Are Bitrate and Capture Cost
cards.angle: Streamed 4D Gaussian splats now play on phones and headsets, so the playback problem is solved. What remains is how much bandwidth, capture work and processing a creator spends to make a scene worth watching.
cards.evidence: Your WebXR tier runs 120K splats per frame at 75 Mbps with keyframe plus delta encoding, with a 15K-splat mode at 17 Mbps, and your Vision Pro app cut bandwidth 10x against your earlier tech. The codec story and the capture-cost story are both told in press coverage; the piece tells them in your words.

cards.title: A 78-Camera Rig for One Theme Park Character
cards.angle: Production 4DGS still needs tens of synchronised cameras and a studio session, which keeps capture out of reach for most productions. The playback side runs on a standalone headset; the capture side is still a soundstage.
cards.evidence: Your PortAventura build used 78 cameras in London, compressed tens of GB to about 850MB per minute, and plays at 72-plus fps on a PICO 4 Ultra Enterprise, while UploadVR reports around 60 cameras and studio sessions from about $15,000 for other captures. The article is what would have to change for productions without that stage.

cards.title: Capture Rigs as Physical AI Training Data
cards.angle: Nvidia's Cosmos 3 (June 2026) trained on 400M real and synthetic videos plus robot action data, and world-model teams want multi-view human motion with depth. The same rig that films a performer can produce it, with conditions.
cards.evidence: Your /data page extends the capture pipeline toward physical AI, listing multi-camera and stereo POV capture with depth, hand tracking and semantic splats. A first article would show exactly what a robotics team receives from one capture (synchronisation, calibration, labels, licensing) and which steps still separate that asset from model training.
